items.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014
items.q: And one of the last guys I used, Alioune Faye, his whole family plays.

ctx.x: Yeah, they just had a fellow at Hamilton last week with an mbira and he basically was saying the same thing, that the scale intonation can actually vary from one village to the next.

Yeah. Which is really, really nice and slick in itself. Because everything has an identity. And I guess for a lot of them, they hear them and they can tell, okay I know that sound, I know where that’s coming from. But it’s the same way with the music, which is interesting too. Because even with the drummers, that’s why with a lot of my students I tell them they have to go — because I got it from Jackie — they have to go study the history of this music. If you really want to play this music and play it well and…

My daughter actually plays in an African drum ensemble in Rochester. And I go to see them. It’s led by a fellow from West Africa. And it would annoy me — the music was incredible but I would get annoyed when I couldn’t put — where’s 1? You know, I’d lose it. And I don’t think I should be annoyed but I kept trying to codify it into something I could feel like I understood.
